content: Losses associated with influenza illness have been studied extensively. Economic analyses conducted in the United States on influenza vaccination for individuals aged over 65 years have demonstrated significant societal cost savings. These studies also report substantial reductions in hospitalizations and mortality rates. Among adults aged 65 years and older, influenza vaccination has been shown to result in net savings per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. For younger age groups, the cost per QALY ranged from $23 to $256. However, further research is necessary to evaluate the relative cost-effectiveness and cost utility of influenza vaccination in children and adults under 65 years of age. Such studies should account for annual variations in influenza attack rates, illness severity, and vaccine efficacy to accurately assess the long-term costs and benefits of annual vaccination programs. One of the national health objectives for 2010 was to achieve a 90% vaccination coverage rate among individuals aged over 65 years. Influenza vaccination coverage in this age group increased from 33% in 1989 to 66% in 1999, surpassing the Healthy People 2000 objective of 60%. The highest recorded vaccination coverage in this group was 68% during the 1999-2000 influenza season, based on data from the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). This survey used the percentage of adults reporting influenza vaccination in the previous 12 months as a proxy measure for vaccine coverage. Individuals categorized as being at high risk for influenza-related complications self-reported one or more of the following conditions: a history of diabetes, emphysema, coronary heart disease, angina, heart attack, or other heart conditions; a cancer diagnosis within the past 12 months (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer) or a history of lymphoma, leukemia, or blood cancer; chronic bronchitis or kidney disease; or an asthma episode or attack in the preceding 12 months. Pregnant women aged 18-44 years without high-risk conditions were also included in certain analyses. Adults employed in healthcare occupations or settings were classified as healthcare workers based on standard occupational and industry categories. Possible reasons for the increase in influenza vaccination levels among individuals aged over 65 years during the 1999-2000 influenza season include greater acceptance of preventive medical services by healthcare practitioners, increased vaccine delivery and administration by providers other than physicians, new information on vaccine effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and safety, and the initiation of Medicare reimbursement for influenza vaccination in 1993. Vaccination coverage increased more rapidly through the mid-1990s, with an average annual percentage increase of 4% from 1988-1989 to 1996-1997, compared to 1% from 1996-1997 to 1999-2000. Since 2000, coverage levels have remained relatively stable. In 2003, estimated national influenza vaccine coverage among individuals aged over 65 years and those aged 50-64 years was 66% and 37%, respectively, based on NHIS data. Among adults with high-risk conditions, vaccination coverage was 24% for those aged 18-49 years and 46% for those aged 50-64 years, both substantially lower than the Healthy People 2000 and 2010 objectives of 60%. Continued annual monitoring is necessary to assess the effects of vaccine supply delays and shortages, changes in vaccination recommendations and target groups, reimbursement rates for vaccine and administration, and other factors influencing vaccination coverage among adults and children. New strategies will be required to improve coverage and achieve the Healthy People 2010 objectives. Reducing racial and ethnic health disparities, including disparities in vaccination coverage, remains a national priority. Although influenza vaccination coverage during the 1999-2000 season reached the highest levels recorded among older Black, Hispanic, and White populations, vaccination rates among Black and Hispanic individuals continue to lag behind those of White individuals.
